extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, especially readers of Northrop Frye's Anatomy of Criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and apply Northrop Frye's Third Essay (Theory of Myths) categories for interpreting literary works: his distinction between dianoia and mythos, archetypal imagery types, the seven levels of reality, the four pregeneric mythoi and their phases, displacement, and character-function relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand-back method (distance to observe archetypal shapes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye's suggestion to 'stand back' from a work to observe its organizing design rather than realistic detail; analogous to viewing a painting from different distances to see brushwork, content, or archetype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use increasing distance to shift analysis from rhetorical/new-critical detail to content and then to organizing archetypal design; the farther back, the more archetypal (e.g., seeing the 'archetype of the Madonna'). This is the methodological starting point for detecting archetypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal primacy of myth
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal patterns are most clearly discernible in myth, since myth inhabits a world of 'pure and abstract literary design' at the pole of total metaphorical identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking structural principles, prioritize mythic texts (undisplaced myth) as exemplars; use myth as the baseline to which displaced forms (romance, mimetic realism) are compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dianoia versus Mythos
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between dianoia (the static structural pattern of imagery and ideas—the literary equivalent of musical key) and mythos (the narrative or processual movement from one imagery-structure to another—the literary equivalent of musical rhythm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze works both synchronically (dianoia: imagery patterns, key) and diachronically (mythos: narrative movement); both perspectives reveal different but related structural information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of archetypal imagery (apocalyptic, demonic, analogical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal imagery divides into apocalyptic, demonic, and analogical kinds; analogical is further subdivided (romantic, high mimetic, low mimetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate imagery on this axis: apocalyptic = undisplaced myth/visionary; demonic = nightmare/hell/parody; analogical = human-form of myth (with three intermediate analogical kinds corresponding to romantic, high mimetic, low mimetic). Use these to read tone and mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven categories/levels of reality (vertical axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye's vertical axis locates imagery across seven 'worlds' or levels: divine, human, animal, vegetable, mineral, fire, and watery (seven categories forming a paradigm of the Great Chain of Being).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map images to these levels to see their vertical relations (e.g., lamb↔city↔tree) and to detect radical identifications at the apocalyptic level; consult Frye's matrices (figures) for typical correspondences of images at each level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical metaphor / apocalyptic identity
rubrics_metrics.description: At the apocalyptic level images are 'radical metaphors' yielding the concrete universal: apocalyptic images can be identical with one another across the seven categories (e.g., Christ as God, man, lamb, tree, temple, water, light).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing apocalyptic imagery, expect cross-level identifications and a collapse of ordinary distinctions; use this to justify readings that treat disparate images as a single apocalyptic symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement (verisimilitude and moral plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Displacement is the movement away from undisplaced myth toward plausibility (verisimilitude) and often toward moral acceptability; displacement masks latent (often disagreeable) content behind manifest, morally acceptable forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for both the manifest (displaced) content and its latent archetypal source; be alert to techniques like 'demonic modulation' where demonic images are recast into morally acceptable forms; failure to recognize displacement leads to faulty interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent vs manifest content (full critical analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'full critical analysis' should consider latent content behind displaced manifest content; latent content is structurally important and often lies nearer undisplaced myth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a psychoanalytic-like attention to underlying desires and repugnant or morally disagreeable material implicit in a text; use latent readings to identify the mythic core lifting a work beyond the merely historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectical and cyclical organizing rhythms
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal criticism rests on two organizing rhythms: a dialectical pattern (movement between poles, e.g., apocalyptic ↔ demonic or innocence ↔ experience) and a cyclical pattern (alternation of success and decline, life and death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both rhythms: dialectical analysis traces tendencies and oppositions; cyclical analysis traces recurrent seasonal/day/life cycles and phases that produce the mythoi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclical imagery and fourfold phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of Frye's seven levels can be analyzed cyclically; within cycles there are four main phases (analogous to seasons, times of day, aspects of water, life periods) which underpin the four mythoi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for quadripartite patterns (spring/summer/fall/winter; morning/noon/evening/night; youth/maturity/old age/death) to locate a work's place in the cyclical scheme and to relate its mood/structure to a mythos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregeneric elements (mythoi): comedy, romance, tragedy, irony/satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye defines four pregeneric narrative categories (mythoi) broader than ordinary genres: comedy, romance, tragedy, and irony/satire (realism). These derive from cyclical and dialectical processes of archetypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify works by their dominant mythos rather than conventional genre labels; identify the prevailing narrative movement, mood, and structural expectations of the relevant mythos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure as central category (plot/shape determines character and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Frye, the structure or shape of a work (determined by its mythos) decides dramatic function; characterization depends on function — 'what a character is follows from what he has to do in the play.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze plot shape and resolution first to derive character types and functions; do not assume character fully determines plot—use structure-to-character inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for comedy (plot pattern and thematic movement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical comic pattern: a young man desires a young woman; desire is obstructed (often by paternal/blocking characters); a plot twist enables desire to be realized; two centers of interest (obstruction and overcoming) and a comic resolution creating a new society; thematic movement from pistis (opinion/illusion) to gnosis (proof/reality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify blocking characters (alazons), comic anagnorisis, festive rituals (weddings, banquets) and the implicit memory of a golden age; determine whether emphasis on obstruction or reconciliation pushes comedy toward satire/realism or romantic comedy respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for romance (quest-adventure and archetypal stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance centers on adventure shaped by a quest; typical romantic plot stages: agon (conflict), pathos (death-struggle), anagnorisis (recognition), and often sparagmos (the hero's disappearance/tearing). The archetypal theme is dragon-killing (hero vs fallen/tyrannical order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the quest structure and its three-four stages; look for heroic exaltation, descent into the monster, and the hero's disappearance as structural markers of romance; map romance imagery to biblical/epic prototypes for full effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy method (music, ritual, dream, lawsuit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye repeatedly employs analogies (music: key/rhythm/ternary form; ritual: seasonal contests; dream: libido quest; lawsuit: pistis→gnosis) to move frames of reference outward and define mythoi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-domain analogies to illuminate narrative structures and themes—but treat analogies as heuristic devices to place works within larger cultural/mythic patterns rather than literal equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character stock types and function-based classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical stock character types derive from dramatic function and include alazon (impostor), eiron (self-deprecator/heroic vice), bomolochos (buffoon), and agroikos (rustic/churl), with numerous subtypes; these categories apply across mythoi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify characters by the narrative role they perform in enabling the structure (blocking, trickster, hero, retreating paterfamilias, etc.); expect variations and subtypes—type informs but does not exhaust lifelikeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six phases per mythos (phase as stage within a mythos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each mythos can be divided into six phases, producing twenty-four distinct narrative structures; phases are not separate literary kinds but broad narrative movements that can apply to parts of works, groups of works, or authorial clusters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate phases using the criteria Frye employs (imagery, theme, plot structure, character, mood, audience perspective) and note that adjacent mythoi phases often merge or correspond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria used to distinguish phases (imagery, theme, plot, character, mood, audience perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye consistently appeals to imagery, theme, plot structure, character types, mood/tone, and occasionally audience perspective to define and distinguish phases within a mythos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning a phase, assemble multiple criteria (e.g., green-world imagery + youthful hero + pastoral mood → second-phase romance/tragedy); single criteria sometimes suffice but cross-check across categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallels and mergers between mythoi and phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjacent mythoi and their phases often blend (e.g., comedy↔satire↔romance; romance may be comic or tragic); Frye emphasizes both contrast and gradual blending, so distinctions are 'tenuous, but not quite a distinction without a difference.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect hybrid works and gradual shifts; map degrees of proximity to poles (apocalyptic vs demonic; ideal vs actual) to explain tonal/structural hybridity rather than forcing rigid genre labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of tone/mood and size of social unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone (festive, idyllic, reflective, or 'penseroso/oracular') and the depicted social unit (from world to small occult societies to individual) are diagnostic criteria for phases and mythoi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include assessment of mood and scope (e.g., large celebratory society = early-phase comic/romance; broken-up small units = sixth-phase contemplative) when categorizing a work's mythic phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological presupposition: literature as a total order of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye assumes structural principles cannot be derived except by conceiving literature as a total order of words—thus archetypal and anagogic criticism presuppose a larger context and seek schematic organizing principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a holistic orientation when applying Frye: look for recurring conventions across literature and Western cultural history rather than isolated textual peculiarities; see the work as part of a system of motifs and myths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of imagery clusters / 'significant constellations'
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye identifies clusters or 'significant constellations' of imagery characteristic of modes (e.g., romantic imagery clusters like chastity/magic, love/form, genesis/work for the three analogical types).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring image-clusters in a text and read them together as an organizing dianoia; these clusters help place a work within a mode or phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of displacement's ethical implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Displacement affects moral readings: apocalyptic imagery is indifferent to conventional morality; as displacement proceeds toward plausibility it often aligns moral with desirable; demonic modulation can reverse customary moral associations of images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting moral valence of an image, account for historical/discursive displacement—do not assume fixed moral associations; consider authorial modulation and cultural context.
